title: Manipulation in sport
excerpt: How to avoid getting hooked and becoming a victim of manipulation at sporting events
body_html:
Sport is essential to our daily lives, with the thrilling moments and unpredictability of competition, and the skill and determination of athletes and other participants. Above all, sport is a powerful driver of social cohesion and development.

Sporting contests are played according to the rules of sporting ethics, based on the principles of honour, fairness and fair competition. However, the integrity of sports competitions, and sporting ethics in general, are substantially threatened by match-fixing and the manipulation of competition results.

These principles do not always guide participants in sports competitions, and the desire for personal enrichment, the powerlessness of decision-makers in sports organisations and the influence of organised crime lead to fraudulent interference with competition results.

Beyond athletes’ results and achievements, whether individual or team, sport also has a financial side, involving sponsorship and advertising contracts, the exploitation of broadcasting rights, ticket sales, organising away matches and so on.

The petty interests of those who fix matches unfortunately cause huge financial losses for everyone involved in sporting events in the broad sense, reputational risks for sports federations, for a particular team or athlete, and sometimes even for the state. What is more, illegally obtained income can be used to finance other illegal activities.

A combination of factors — the petty desire to get rich quickly, weak management and leadership in sports organisations, easily accessible betting platforms open to mass use, insufficient attention and involvement of law-enforcement bodies in corruption in sport, and the use of sport by organised crime, including transnational crime, to further its own interests — has created a situation in which this threat keeps growing.

The popularity of sports competitions with the public, significant financial investment and the capacity to affect a country’s image create an environment for specific forms of corruption in sport.

One of them is the manipulation of sports competition results. This form of fraud is found in practically every sport in which large sums of money are invested, from traditional sports to modern ones such as esports (cybersport). Match-fixing is often organised by criminal groups running illegal bookmakers, whose intermediaries corrupt athletes, coaches, sports managers or referees to influence competition results one way or another and then make substantial profits from betting.

The worldwide growth in table tennis’s popularity, numerous online broadcasts of events and the globalisation of sports betting have quickly generated interest in the sport and a significant volume of bets. This is especially true in Eastern Europe, where table tennis is among the most popular sports with bookmakers, after football and tennis. While in football it is extremely hard to track the physical and mental state of each team’s 11 starting players, in table tennis this is far easier — watching just 2-3 matches of a given player is enough to analyse their performance and mental state.

Betting turnover on table tennis events worldwide now runs into millions of dollars, and when such impressive sums are at stake, people inevitably appear who try to manipulate sporting results. That means there are inevitably cases among table tennis players of being tempted to collude with these fraudsters.

It might seem pointless to “throw” matches when, for example, the knockout system does not allow the losing player to continue in the tournament, and every professional tournament, even in the Challenger series, has a considerable prize fund. In this case, however, the motivation is not to raise one’s rating and be rewarded for a tough tournament battle, but to easily earn in a single attempt as much money as in 3-5 tournaments, prize money included. Obviously, “throwing” a match takes no special skill or effort — a small mistake, and the ball goes long or into the net on the key points.

Fraudsters identify and select potential “victims” among players, contact them, negotiate with them and then sell the information about the fixed match to those ready to bet, or bet themselves. In the past there were athletes who regularly took part in match-fixing, and fraudsters could “order” a rigged match from them. Today, however, many mechanisms have been developed and put in place to detect match-fixing, and as a rule an athlete’s “career” ends in disgrace after the first leak.

Despite considerable attention, the question of holding participants accountable and explaining the consequences of match-fixing remains insufficiently studied, and the lack of adequate regulatory instruments keeps creating new precedents.
